newsitem.title: FINLAND: Nokia 1996 seen undramatic, profit-takers may lurk.
newsitem.headline: Nokia 1996 seen undramatic, profit-takers may lurk.

text.p: Finnish telecoms major Nokia Oy's 1996 report due on Thursday is not expected to bring any drama, but strong price gains since last summer make Nokia shares vulnerable to profit-taking, analysts say.

Nokia's share has risen over 200 percent in six months to approach the 340.00 markka life-high set in September 1995 before it plunged on the company's logistics problems and investor mistrust in the management.
On Wednesday, it traded warily around 321.00-324.00 markka.

The median forecast for Nokia's fourth quarter profit is 1.62 billion markka, up from 1.1 billion in the third quarter, putting the full-year profit at 3.85 billion markka, well below the record 4.93 billion profit set in 1995.

Forecasts for the full-year 1997 profit before tax and minorities range from 3.30 billion to 4.92 billion markka. The report is due around 1300/1100 GMT and Nokia will hold a news conference half an hour later.
"There are some very optimistic forecasts around," said Susan Anthony, an analyst at Schroder in London, adding that some profit-taking could be expected.

Anthony said Nokia's rival Ericsson's report on Tuesday -- pre-tax profit up 33 percent at 10.2 billion crowns -- was "a good set of figures" and that she had upgraded her forecast for Ericsson, rating it higher than Nokia due to the risk of profit-taking.
But she said the telecoms sector was still "very exciting".
Postipankki analyst Ilkka Salonen agreed that some may want to take profits, but said he saw far greater upside in Nokia's shares around the time of the profit announcement.
"The downside risk is smaller. There is a chance that Nokia will give stronger-than-expected comments," Salonen said.
He said he would look for encouraging comments on Nokia's fixed network business, where he expected growth as liberalisation will open European markets for new telephone operators.
"Nokia has been particularly strong in the market for second operators," he said.

Nokia shares wobbled on Tuesday when Ericsson said price pressures on all its products would be similar in 1997 as last year, but Goldman Sachs analyst Richard Kramer warned against focusing too much on single price pressure figures since segmentation is far more important for mobile phone makers.
For instance, a 25 percent fall in the price of Nokia's top segment product, the 9000 Communicator, is worse than a 10 percent drop in a regular high-volume mobile phone.
Analysts hope to see a recovery in Nokia's infrastructure business which slumped below expectations in Q3.
Kramer said the telecommunications infrastructure was growing strongly and order backlogs were massive, making absolute performance much more important than market share comments.
"If Nokia's (1996) infrastructure sales are above 14 billion markka, that's good," he said.

In 1995, Nokia's infrastructure arm Nokia Telecommunications posted a 2.7 billion markka operating profit on 10.3 billion markka net sales, while Nokia Mobile Phones' profit was 1.75 billion markka on 16.1 billion markka net sales.
Nokia does not report interim operating profits by division. The telecommunications arm's nine-month net sales were 9.1 billion markka while Mobile Phones net sales totalled 14.4 billion.
Arctos analyst Jyrki Hilli said he was encouraged by Ericsson's forecast of 480 million cellular subscribers worldwide all brands included in the year 2000, up from 137 million at end-1996.
"The forecast is higher than any other manufacturers' so far," he said, adding his own forecast was 430 million.
